CS2 Final Project – Data Explorer (Sorting & Searching Capstone)

1. Project Overview

For the last part of the semester, you’ll build a small “Data Explorer” program in Python.

Your program will:

  • Load a dataset from a file (CSV or text)

  • Store it using lists, dictionaries, and classes

  • Let a user search, sort, and filter the data through a simple menu

  • Create at least one plot to visualize something interesting

  • Handle bad input and file errors gracefully

This is not meant to be a huge stressful project. It’s a chance to use the tools you already know (loops, functions, classes, files, exceptions, searching, sorting, plotting) in one coherent program.

You will work individually but we’ll spend several class days doing pair programming and show-and-tell so you can get help and share ideas.

2. Learning Goals

By the end of this project, you should be able to:

  1. Design a small Python program using functions, modules, and classes.

  2. Use lists and dictionaries to store structured data.

  3. Read from and write to files in a safe way.

  4. Implement and use simple searching and sorting algorithms.

  5. Add basic exception handling to make your program robust.

  6. Create a simple plot from your data and interpret it.

  7. Talk about your design choices and reflect on what you learned.

3. What You Will Build

You will choose a dataset (or use one provided) such as:

  • Movies (title, year, rating, genre)

  • Songs (title, artist, length, rating)

  • Students (name, major, GPA, graduation year)

  • Books, video games, sports stats, etc.

Then you’ll build a terminal-based Data Explorer that supports at least:

  • Loading the data from a file into memory

  • Showing a list of records (possibly limited to top N)

  • Searching for records by some key (title, name, ID, etc.)

  • Sorting the data by at least one field

  • Saving some results (for example, a filtered or sorted subset) to a file

  • Generating one simple plot (e.g., a bar chart or histogram)

4. Project Requirements

4.1 Data & Model

  • Your program must read from at least one input file (CSV or reasonably structured text).

  • Create at least one class to represent a record, e.g.:

    class Movie:
    def __init__(self, title, year, rating, genre):
        ...

  • Store your data in a list of objects (or dictionaries).

4.2 Program Structure

  • Your code must be split into at least two modules:

    • models.py – classes and any data-related helper functions

    • app.py – user interface (menus, main loop)

  • Use functions to organize your code. Avoid writing all logic in one giant main().

4.3 Core Features

Your program must support:

  1. Menu-based interface

    • A loop that repeatedly shows options (list data, search, sort, plot, quit).

    • Clear prompts and labels.

  2. Searching

    • Implement at least one search algorithm yourself:

      • Linear search is fine.

      • If you want to use binary search, make sure the data is sorted first.

    • Use your search in at least one menu option (e.g., “Find movie by title”).

  3. Sorting

    • Implement at least one simple sort yourself (e.g. insertion sort or selection sort).

    • Also demonstrate Python’s built-in sorted() on the same data.

    • You should be able to tell the user which sort is being used in each option.

  4. Files

    • Use with open(...) to read your data file.

    • Provide at least one option that writes out data (e.g. saving a filtered or sorted list to a new file).

  5. Exceptions & Robustness

    • Use try/except to handle:

      • Invalid user input (e.g. non-integer menu choices)

      • Missing or unreadable file

    • Program should not crash on simple user mistakes.

  6. Plotting

    • Use a plotting library (such as matplotlib) to draw at least one plot related to your data:

      • Example: histogram of ratings, bar chart of counts per genre/major, etc.

    • The plot can appear in a separate window or be saved as an image file.

4.4 Reflection

Write a short reflection (roughly ½–1 page) that answers:

  • What data did you choose, and why?

  • Which searching and sorting strategies did you implement?

  • One thing that surprised you while building the project.

  • If you had one more week, what would you add or improve?

You may submit this as a text file, PDF, or Canvas text entry.

4.5 Optional Extensions (Bonus / Stretch)

These are not required, but can earn bonus credit and make your project more interesting:

  • Inheritance (e.g. MediaItem base class with Movie and Song subclasses).

  • Use binary search on a sorted list.

  • Add multiple plots or more advanced visualizations.

  • Add simple unit tests for your search/sort functions.

  • Use basic recursion somewhere reasonable (not forced).

5. Timeline & In-Class Plan

This is a Monday/Wednesday/Friday class.

Week 1 – Kickoff & Planning (This Week)

Day 1 (Today) – Project Overview & Kickoff

  • Project handout and explanation.

  • In-class:

    • Choose or explore possible datasets.

    • Sketch your data model (what fields each record has).

    • Start a basic project folder with app.py and models.py.

Day 2 (Wednesday) – Pair Programming #1

  • Focus: data loading + basic menu.

  • In-class goals:

    • Define your main data class in models.py.

    • Write code to load the file into a list of objects.

    • Add a simple main menu and an option to print the first few records.

Day 3 (Friday) – Project Plan Show & Tell

  • Each student (or small team if you’re sharing data) will very briefly:

    • Introduce their dataset.

    • Explain their planned features (search + sort + plot).

    • Show whatever they already have working (even if it’s just data loading).

Week 2 – Thanksgiving Week (Campus Partially Closed)

  • Monday: Optional office hours / help session.

  • Wednesday & Friday: No class (Thanksgiving break).

No new required work is assigned this week.
You may use this time to make progress if you want, but you are not required to.

Week 3 – Build, Polish, and Demo (Week After Thanksgiving / Dead Week)

Day 4 (Monday) – Pair Programming #2

  • Focus: searching and sorting.

  • In-class goals:

    • Implement your required search function.

    • Implement your required sort function.

    • Integrate both into your menu.

Day 5 (Wednesday) – Pair Programming #3

  • Focus: exceptions, plotting, and polish.

  • In-class goals:

    • Wrap user input and file operations with try/except.

    • Add at least one plot.

    • Clean up your menu and output formatting.

    • Work on your short reflection.

Day 6 (Friday) – Final Show & Tell

  • Each student gives a 3–5 minute demo:

    • Run your program and show:

      • Data loading

      • One search

      • One sort

      • Your plot

    • Share one thing you’re proud of and one challenge you hit.

  • Final project files and reflection are due Friday night (or whatever deadline your instructor sets).

6. Deliverables

By the final deadline, you will submit:

  1. Code

    • All .py files needed to run your project.

    • Your data file(s) (unless they are huge; in that case, include a small sample).

  2. Reflection

    • ½–1 page answering the questions in Section 4.4.

  3. Demo

    • In-class show-and-tell on the two Fridays:

      • Week 1 Friday – project plan.

      • Week 3 Friday – final project demo.

7. Grading Rubric (100 points + optional bonus)

1. Core Functionality (50 points)

  • Loads data from file into appropriate structures (10)

  • Menu-driven interface with at least three meaningful options (10)

  • Working search feature using your own implementation (10)

  • Working sort feature using your own implementation + use of sorted() somewhere (10)

  • Ability to save some results to a file (10)

2. Use of CS2 Concepts (25 points)

  • Proper use of at least one class to model records (10)

  • Use of modules and functions to organize code (5)

  • Basic exception handling for input and files (5)

  • At least one plot generated from your data (5)

3. Code Quality & Style (15 points)

  • Reasonable variable and function names (5)

  • Code is broken into functions instead of one giant block (5)

  • Comments/docstrings where needed; code is readable (5)

4. Communication & Reflection (10 points)

  • Participation in the two show-and-tell days (5)

  • Clear, honest written reflection turned in on time (5)

Bonus / Stretch Features (up to +10 points)

  • Any combination of optional extensions (inheritance, binary search, extra plots, tests, recursion, etc.) that are well-implemented and documented.

Please email me at jeremy.evert@swosu.edu if there is anything unexpected. Or you can text me at 785-443-0967. 

Please do 6.18 over unit tests as part of your 3 codes for this week.

Grading Structure:

Please do 3 problems from this week’s Chapter. You may substitute a problem of your own creation based on that week’s chapter. 

Base Points: Criteria (not stacking)
25 points: Demonstration of effort, but no working codes
50 points: Have one programming solution working
75 points: Have two programming solutions working
100 points: Have three programming solutions working
    Bonus: (Stacking)
10 points: Some improvement on one problem.
20 points: Some improvement on two problems.
30 points: All three programming solutions working with some improvement on three problems.
25 points: You record a video and talk about how or why you worked your problems the way you did
50 points: Push your code to the SWOSU shared repository and post your link: https://github.com/swosu/SwosuCsPythonExamples/tree/main/Student_Codes
You will need to post your link in the discussion to receive bonus points for this.
25 points: Anyone that presents during class.

 

Suggested Problems:

# Problem : )

6.18 Lab training: Unit tests to evaluate your program

Auto-graded programming assignments may use a Unit test to test small parts of a program. Unlike a Compare output test, which evaluates your program's output for specific input values, a Unit test evaluates individual functions to determines if each function:

  • is named correctly and has the correct parameters and return type
  • calculates and returns the correct value (or prints the correct output)

The zyLabs auto-grader runs main.py as a script. In main.py, the line if __name__ == '__main__': is used to separate the main code from the functions' code so that each function can be unit tested. Enter statements to be run as the main code under if __name__ == '__main__':. Indent the statements so the statements belong to the if block. Refer to the subsection Importing modules and executing scripts under section Module basics for more information about running a program as a script.

Note: Do not remove if __name__ == '__main__': from the code. Otherwise, the unit tests will fail even though the program produces the correct output.

This example lab uses multiple unit tests to test the kilo_to_pounds() function.

Complete a program that takes a weight in kilograms as input, converts the weight to pounds, and then outputs the weight in pounds. 1 kilogram = 2.204 pounds (lbs).

The program must define the following function:
def kilo_to_pounds(kilos) - take kilos as a parameter, convert kilos from kilograms to pounds, and return the weight in pounds.

Ex: If the input of the program is:

10

10 is passed to kilo_to_pounds() and the output of the program is:

22.040 lbs

The program below has an error in the kilo_to_pounds() function.

  1. Try submitting the program for grading (click "Submit mode", then "Submit for grading"). Notice that the first two test cases fail, but the third test case passes. The first test case fails because the program outputs the result from the kilo_to_pounds() function, which has an error. The second test case uses a Unit test to test the kilo_to_pounds() function, which fails.

  2. Change the kilo_to_pounds() function to multiply the variable kilos by 2.204, instead of dividing. The return statement should be: return (kilos * 2.204). Submit again. Now the test cases should all pass.

Note: A common error is to mistype a function name with the incorrect capitalization. Function names are case sensitive, so if a lab program asks for a kilo_to_pounds() function, a kilo_To_Pounds() function that works for you in "Develop mode" will result in a failed unit test. The unit test will not be able to find kilo_to_pounds().

# Starter Code :

def kilo_to_pounds(kilos):
    # This statement intentionally has an error. 
    return (kilos / 2.204)


# Main part of the program starts here. Do not remove the line below.
if __name__ == '__main__':
    kilos = float(input())
    
    pounds = kilo_to_pounds(kilos)
    print(f'{pounds:.3f} lbs')

Write a function driving_cost() with input parameters miles_per_gallon, dollars_per_gallon, and miles_driven, that returns the dollar cost to drive those miles. All items are of type float. The function called with arguments (20.0, 3.1599, 50.0) returns 7.89975.

Define that function in a program whose inputs are the car's miles per gallon and the price of gas in dollars per gallon (both float). Output the gas cost for 10 miles, 50 miles, and 400 miles, by calling your driving_cost() function three times.

Output each floating-point value with two digits after the decimal point, which can be achieved as follows:
print(f'{your_value:.2f}')

Ex: If the input is:

20.0
3.1599

the output is:

1.58
7.90
63.20

Your program must define and call a function:
def driving_cost(miles_per_gallon, dollars_per_gallon, miles_driven)

A pedometer treats walking 1 step as walking 2.5 feet. Define a function named feet_to_steps that takes a float as a parameter, representing the number of feet walked, and returns an integer that represents the number of steps walked. Then, write a main program that reads the number of feet walked as an input, calls function feet_to_steps() with the input as an argument, and outputs the number of steps as an integer.

Use floating-point arithmetic to perform the conversion.

Ex: If the input is:

150.5

the output is:

60

The program must define and call the following function:
def feet_to_steps(user_feet)

6.21 LAB: Convert to binary - functions

Write a program that takes in a positive integer as input, and outputs a string of 1's and 0's representing the integer in binary. For an integer x, the algorithm is:

As long as x is greater than 0
   Output x % 2 (remainder is either 0 or 1)
   x = x // 2

Note: The above algorithm outputs the 0's and 1's in reverse order. You will need to write a second function to reverse the string.

Ex: If the input is:

6

the output is:

110

The program must define and call the following two functions. Define a function named int_to_reverse_binary() that takes an integer as a parameter and returns a string of 1's and 0's representing the integer in binary (in reverse). Define a function named string_reverse() that takes an input string as a parameter and returns a string representing the input string in reverse.

6.22 LAB: Swapping variables

Define a function named swap_values that takes four integers as parameters and swaps the first with the second, and the third with the fourth values. Then write a main program that reads four integers from input, calls function swap_values() to swap the values, and prints the swapped values on a single line separated with spaces.

Ex: If the input is:

3
8
2
4

function swap_values() returns and the main program outputs:

8 3 4 2

6.23 LAB: Fibonacci sequence

The Fibonacci sequence begins with 0 and then 1 follows. All subsequent values are the sum of the previous two, ex: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Complete the fibonacci() function, which has an index, n (starting at 0), as a parameter and returns the nth value in the sequence. Any negative index values should return -1.

Ex: If the input is:

7

the output is:

fibonacci(7) is 13

23.1 LAB: Track laps to miles

lab activity
23.1.1: LAB: Track laps to miles
open_in_newfullscreen0 / 10

One lap around a standard high-school running track is exactly 0.25 miles. Define a function named laps_to_miles that takes a number of laps as a parameter, and returns the number of miles. Then, write a main program that takes a number of laps as an input, calls function laps_to_miles() to calculate the number of miles, and outputs the number of miles.

Output each floating-point value with two digits after the decimal point, which can be achieved as follows:
print(f'{your_value:.2f}')

Ex: If the input is:

7.6

the output is:

1.90

Ex: If the input is:

2.2

the output is:

0.55

The program must define and call the following function:
def laps_to_miles(user_laps)

23.2 LAB: Max magnitude

lab activity
23.2.1: LAB: Max magnitude
open_in_newfullscreen0 / 10

Write a function max_magnitude() with three integer parameters that returns the largest magnitude value. Use the function in the main program that takes three integer inputs and outputs the largest magnitude value.

Ex: If the inputs are:

5
7
9

function max_magnitude() returns and the main program outputs:

9

Ex: If the inputs are:

-17
-8
-2

function max_magnitude() returns and the main program outputs:

-17

Note: The function does not just return the largest value, which for -17 -8 -2 would be -2. Though not necessary, you may use the built-in absolute value function to determine the max magnitude, but you must still output the input number (Ex: Output -17, not 17).

Your program must define and call the following function:
def max_magnitude(user_val1, user_val2, user_val3)

23.3 LAB: A jiffy

lab activity
23.3.1: LAB: A jiffy
open_in_newfullscreen0 / 10

In computer animation, a "jiffy" is commonly defined as 1/100th of a second. Define a function named jiffies_to_seconds that takes the number of "jiffies" as a parameter, and returns the number of seconds. Then, write a main program that reads the number of jiffies (float) as an input, calls function jiffies_to_seconds() with the input as argument, and outputs the number of seconds.

Output each floating-point value with three digits after the decimal point, which can be achieved as follows:
print(f'{your_value:.3f}')

Ex: If the input is:

15.25

the output is:

0.152

The program must define and call the following function:
def jiffies_to_seconds(user_jiffies)

23.4 LAB: Leap year - functions

lab activity
23.4.1: LAB: Leap year - functions
open_in_newfullscreen0 / 10

A common year in the modern Gregorian Calendar consists of 365 days. In reality, Earth takes longer to rotate around the sun. To account for the difference in time, every 4 years, a leap year takes place. A leap year is when a year has 366 days: An extra day, February 29th. The requirements for a given year to be a leap year are:

1) The year must be divisible by 4

# Problem : )

6.18 Lab training: Unit tests to evaluate your program

Auto-graded programming assignments may use a Unit test to test small parts of a program. Unlike a Compare output test, which evaluates your program's output for specific input values, a Unit test evaluates individual functions to determines if each function:

  • is named correctly and has the correct parameters and return type
  • calculates and returns the correct value (or prints the correct output)

The zyLabs auto-grader runs main.py as a script. In main.py, the line if __name__ == '__main__': is used to separate the main code from the functions' code so that each function can be unit tested. Enter statements to be run as the main code under if __name__ == '__main__':. Indent the statements so the statements belong to the if block. Refer to the subsection Importing modules and executing scripts under section Module basics for more information about running a program as a script.

Note: Do not remove if __name__ == '__main__': from the code. Otherwise, the unit tests will fail even though the program produces the correct output.

This example lab uses multiple unit tests to test the kilo_to_pounds() function.

Complete a program that takes a weight in kilograms as input, converts the weight to pounds, and then outputs the weight in pounds. 1 kilogram = 2.204 pounds (lbs).

The first test case fails because the program outputs the result from the kilo_to_pounds() function, which has an error. The second test case uses a Unit test to test the kilo_to_pounds() function, which fails.

  2. Change the kilo_to_pounds() function to multiply the variable kilos by 2.204, instead of dividing. The return statement should be: return (kilos * 2.204). Submit again. Now the test cases should all pass.

Note: A common error is to mistype a function name with the incorrect capitalization. Function names are case sensitive, so if a lab program asks for a kilo_to_pounds() function, a kilo_To_Pounds() function that works for you in "Develop mode" will result in a failed unit test. A common year in the modern Gregorian Calendar consists of 365 days. In reality, Earth takes longer to rotate around the sun. To account for the difference in time, every 4 years, a leap year takes place. A leap year is when a year has 366 days: An extra day, February 29th. The requirements for a given year to be a leap year are:

1) The year must be divisible by 4

2) If the year is a century year (1700, 1800, etc.), the year must be evenly divisible by 400; therefore, both 1700 and 1800 are not leap years

Some example leap years are 1600, 1712, and 2016.

def read_customer_data(filename):
    """Read and return data from filename as a list of lists (name, state, debt)"""
    names = []
    states = []
    debts = []

    for row in rows:
        row = row.split(',')
        names.append(row[0])
        states.append(row[1])
        debts.append(float(row[2].strip()))
    return names, states, debts

def read_customer_data(filename):
    """Read and return data from filename as a list of lists (name, state, debt)"""
    names = []
    states = []
    debts = []

    for row in rows:
        row = row.split(',')
        names.append(row[0])
        states.append(row[1])
        debts.append(float(row[2].strip()))
    return names, states, debts

assignments.description:
Introduction to Data Visualization – Programming Assignment

Course: COMSC 2073 Data Visualization
Estimated Time: ~1 Hour
Objective:
This assignment introduces you to data visualization using Python. You will write code to generate simple visualizations with popular libraries such as Matplotlib, Seaborn, and Plotly. By completing this, you’ll gain hands-on experience creating visual representations of data and start exploring key Python tools for data visualization.

Prerequisites

Make sure you have Python installed and the following libraries available. You can install them using:

bash
Copy code
pip install matplotlib seaborn plotly pandas

Assignment Instructions

Part 1: Setup and Basic Line Plot with Matplotlib (15 minutes)

  1. Import the necessary libraries:
python
Copy code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd
  1. Create a DataFrame with the following sales data:
python
Copy code
data = { 'Month': ['January', 'February', 'March', 'April', 'May'], 'Sales': [2500, 3200, 2800, 4000, 3500] } df = pd.DataFrame(data)
  1. Write a Python script to generate a line plot showing the sales trend over the months.
    • Add labels to the x-axis and y-axis, and give the chart a title.

Expected Output:
A line chart with "Months" on the x-axis, "Sales (in USD)" on the y-axis, and the title "Monthly Sales Trend".

Part 2: Creating a Bar Plot with Seaborn (20 minutes)

  1. Import Seaborn and use it to create a bar plot of the same sales data.
    • Customize the colors and add labels.

Sample Code:

python
Copy code
import seaborn as sns sns.set(style="whitegrid") plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6)) sns.barplot(x='Month', y='Sales', data=df, palette='Blues') plt.title('Monthly Sales - Bar Plot') plt.show()
  1. Add comments in your code explaining the key steps (e.g., setting the style, adjusting figure size, adding labels).

Part 3: Interactive Plot with Plotly (25 minutes)

  1. Use the Plotly library to create an interactive line chart.
    • The chart should display the same sales trend, but with tooltips showing exact sales values when hovering over points.

Sample Code:

python
Copy code
import plotly.express as px fig = px.line(df, x='Month', y='Sales', title='Monthly Sales Trend (Interactive)') fig.show()
  1. Experiment with Plotly’s features:
    • Try changing the line color.
    • Add markers at each data point.

Bonus Task (Optional)

  • Use Seaborn to create a scatter plot with random data (e.g., x as product prices and y as units sold).
  • Use Plotly to generate a pie chart showing the proportion of sales per month.

Submission Instructions

  • Submit a Python script (.py file) or a Jupyter notebook (.ipynb) containing all your code and visualizations.
  • Include comments in your code to explain what each part does.

Assessment Criteria

  • Correctness: Does the code run without errors and generate the expected visualizations?
  • Completeness: Have you completed all three parts?
  • Code Quality: Are your code and comments well-organized?
  • Visualization Quality: Are the visualizations clear, labeled correctly, and visually appealing?

This assignment will give you practical experience with essential Python libraries for data visualization and familiarize you with both static and interactive plots. These skills will form the foundation for your future data visualization projects.

    right_pos = j + 1

            left_pos = left_pos + 1

        merge_pos = merge_pos + 1

    merge_pos = 0
    while merge_pos < merged_size:

        merge_sort(numbers, j + 1, k)

Binary search can be implemented as a recursive algorithm. Each call makes a recursive call on one-half of the list the call received as an argument.

Complete the recursive function binary_search() with the following specifications:

  1. Parameters:

  2. Return value:
    • if found, the index within the list where the target is located
    • -1 if target is not found

The algorithm begins by choosing an index midway between the lower and upper bounds.

  1. If target == nums[index] return index

    • If nums[index] < target, search the list from index + 1 to upper
    • If nums[index] > target, search the list from lower to index - 1

The list must be ordered, but duplicates are allowed.

    30.1 Introduction to data science

    Data science

    Data science is an interdisciplinary field focused on discovering patterns and describing relationships using data. Data science uses techniques from computer science and statistics. Data scientists use computers to write code and store, modify, and visualize large datasets. Data scientists can also build, test, and interpret a data model, a representation of a real-life system that organizes data elements and informs how the elements relate to one another. Ex: The FBI's Most Wanted list is a model that contains data elements such as eye color, hair color, known accomplices, etc. related to each suspect on the list. The data model can be used to make predictions for new data.

    Datasets

    Data scientists uncover patterns and make predictions from datasets. A dataset is a collection of information. Datasets consist of features and instances.     Volume

    Data scientists deal with very large amounts of data. In the past 20 years, the volume of global data has increased exponentially. Data scientists use specialized tools and software to work with big datasets, such as:

    • Apache Spark and Hadoop, two open-source platforms for storing and analyzing large amounts of data.

    Velocity

    Big data grows at a high velocity as datasets are continually updated. Data scientists use several techniques to account for updating data.

    • Models and analyses implemented using code are reproducible: code can be updated and quickly re-run. Code can also be shared with others. Analyses done in software, like Excel, may be more difficult for others to reproduce.
    • Analyses are automated to run at a specific time, such as once per week. Automation is useful if the model isn't likely to change over time, just the data.
    • Data scientists use version control to make sure that new versions of software or coding packages don't affect the analysis.

      30.2 Data science life cycle

      Data science life cycle

      The data science life cycle is a five-step process for completing a research project using data. In some organizations, data scientists are involved in every step of the data science life cycle. In other organizations, data scientists specialize in a single step such as visualization or modeling. Data scientists may revisit steps in the life cycle throughout a single project.

      Table 30.2.1: Data science life cycle.
      Step Description
      Step 1: Gathering data Identify available and relevant data; gather new data if needed.
      Step 2: Cleaning data Reformat datasets, create new features, and address missing values.
      Step 3: Exploring data Create data visualizations and calculate summary statistics to explore potential relationships in the dataset.
      Step 4: Modeling data Use modeling skills and content knowledge to fit and evaluate models, measure relationships, and make predictions.
      Step 5: Interpreting data Describe and interpret conclusions from data through written reports and presentations.

      Step 1: Gathering data

      Data scientists start a project by determining what data is available and what additional data is needed. Datasets may be available in structured or unstructured form. Structured data is stored in a pre-defined format, typically with features stored in columns and instances in rows. Ex: A database is a collection of organized information stored in a computer system. Data stored in databases, or in tables, is considered structured.

      Unstructured data does not have a predefined format and is difficult for humans to interpret. Instead, unstructured data points may contain multiple pieces of information that are converted to a structured form before analysis. Ex: Audio files, videos, images, and text are considered unstructured. Unstructured files may be stored in a database; however, the actual image or audio file itself does not have an organized structure.

      Data scientists may work with structured and unstructured data during a single project.

      Step 4: Modeling data

      Data scientists use content knowledge to select possible models based on a dataset's features. No model is ideal for every situation, which means data scientists must try several models before making a selection.

      Models that predict a feature with known values in the original dataset are supervised models.

      • Classification models predict categorical features.
      • Regression models predict numerical features.
      Unsupervised models look for hidden groups or patterns in the dataset rather than predicting a known feature.

        30.3 Introduction to Python for data science

        Advantages/disadvantages of Python for data science

        Python is one of the most popular languages for data science due to the language's high-level nature, portability, and broad community support. The readability of the language, and the portability of running a Python script easily on different computers, enables collaboration that outweighs performance concerns. Additionally, industry professionals frequently contribute free and high-quality packages for data science that are widely used.

        Table 30.3.1: Advantages and disadvantages of Python for data science.
        Advantages Disadvantages
        Readability: Python reads like English, and functions from the same library use consistent syntax. Consistency: Different libraries may have different syntax conventions.
        Popularity: Python is popular in data science and elsewhere in industry, which means resources for learning Python are widely available. Memory: Python uses more computer memory than other programming languages.
        Innovation: New data science models and technologies are constantly added to Python. Speed: Other programming languages such as Julia perform computations on datasets more quickly than Python.
        Feedback?

        True

        Feedback?

        Common data science packages

        Many Python packages exist for data manipulation, visualization, and modeling. Different packages provide different functionality, so a data science project will use multiple packages. Ex: Imagine a scientist wants to classify hawk populations in Iowa from a large dataset. First the data is loaded into special data structures using pandas, then classification algorithms are run from scikit-learn, and then the results are visualized using seaborn. The unique capabilities of each package provide a data scientist with a comprehensive set of tools for almost any task.

        numpy np NumPy includes functions and classes that aid in numerical computation. NumPy is used in many other data science packages.
        pandas pd pandas provides methods and classes for tabular and time-series data.
        sklearn sk scikit-learn provides implementations of many machine learning algorithms with a uniform syntax for preprocessing data, specifying models, fitting models with cross-validation, and assessing models.
        matplotlib.pyplot plt Matplotlib allows the creation of data visualizations in Python. The functions mostly expect NumPy arrays.
        seaborn sns seaborn also allows the creation of data visualizations but works better with pandas DataFrame objects.
        scipy.stats sp.stats SciPy provides algorithms and functions for computing problems that arise in science, engineering and statistics. scipy.stats provides the functions for statistics.
        statsmodels sm statsmodels adds functionality to Python to estimate many different kinds of statistical models, make inferences from those models, and explore data.

          30.4 Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks

          Jupyter

          Jupyter is an interactive development environment (IDE) for writing and testing code in data science and scientific computing. In Jupyter, code is written in an interactive document called a Jupyter notebook. A notebook contains cells, which organize code, text, and output all in one place for testing, presenting, and sharing. The three types of cells are code cells, markdown (text) cells, and raw (output) cells. Each cell can be run independently.

    30.1 Introduction to data science

    Data science

    Data science is an interdisciplinary field focused on discovering patterns and describing relationships using data. Data science uses techniques from computer science and statistics. Data scientists use computers to write code and store, modify, and visualize large datasets. Data scientists can also build, test, and interpret a data model, a representation of a real-life system that organizes data elements and informs how the elements relate to one another. Ex: The FBI's Most Wanted list is a model that contains data elements such as eye color, hair color, known accomplices, etc. related to each suspect on the list. The data model can be used to make predictions for new data.

    Datasets

    Data scientists uncover patterns and make predictions from datasets. A dataset is a collection of information. Datasets consist of features and instances. A feature, or variable, is a characteristic that can be measured or observed on an observational unit. Features are recorded for individual instances, or observational units, in the dataset. Instances are also called data points or observations.

    Volume

    Data scientists deal with very large amounts of data. In the past 20 years, the volume of global data has increased exponentially. Data scientists use specialized tools and software to work with big datasets, such as:

    • Apache Spark and Hadoop, two open-source platforms for storing and analyzing large amounts of data.
    • Cloudera, software for cloud-based data storage and management.

    Cloud-based storage, like Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure, makes big data more manageable by spreading out datasets across different storage locations and servers. When a part of a dataset is needed, cloud-based systems load only that part. The rest of the dataset is left alone until needed, saving computational time.

    Velocity

    Big data grows at a high velocity as datasets are continually updated. Data scientists use several techniques to account for updating data.

    • Models and analyses implemented using code are reproducible: code can be updated and quickly re-run. Code can also be shared with others. Analyses done in software, like Excel, may be more difficult for others to reproduce.
    • Analyses are automated to run at a specific time, such as once per week. Automation is useful if the model isn't likely to change over time, just the data.
    • Data scientists use version control to make sure that new versions of software or coding packages don't affect the analysis.

      30.2 Data science life cycle

      Data science life cycle

      The data science life cycle is a five-step process for completing a research project using data. In some organizations, data scientists are involved in every step of the data science life cycle. In other organizations, data scientists specialize in a single step such as visualization or modeling. Data scientists may revisit steps in the life cycle throughout a single project.

      Table 30.2.1: Data science life cycle.
      Step Description
      Step 1: Gathering data Identify available and relevant data; gather new data if needed.
      Step 2: Cleaning data Reformat datasets, create new features, and address missing values.
      Step 3: Exploring data Create data visualizations and calculate summary statistics to explore potential relationships in the dataset.
      Step 4: Modeling data Use modeling skills and content knowledge to fit and evaluate models, measure relationships, and make predictions.
      Step 5: Interpreting data Describe and interpret conclusions from data through written reports and presentations.

      Step 1: Gathering data

      Data scientists start a project by determining what data is available and what additional data is needed. Datasets may be available in structured or unstructured form. Structured data is stored in a pre-defined format, typically with features stored in columns and instances in rows. Ex: A database is a collection of organized information stored in a computer system. Data stored in databases, or in tables, is considered structured.

      Unstructured data does not have a predefined format and is difficult for humans to interpret. Instead, unstructured data points may contain multiple pieces of information that are converted to a structured form before analysis. Ex: Audio files, videos, images, and text are considered unstructured. Unstructured files may be stored in a database; however, the actual image or audio file itself does not have an organized structure.

      Data scientists may work with structured and unstructured data during a single project.

      Step 4: Modeling data

      Data scientists use content knowledge to select possible models based on a dataset's features. No model is ideal for every situation, which means data scientists must try several models before making a selection.

      Models that predict a feature with known values in the original dataset are supervised models.

      • Classification models predict categorical features.
      • Regression models predict numerical features.
      Unsupervised models look for hidden groups or patterns in the dataset rather than predicting a known feature.

        30.3 Introduction to Python for data science

        Advantages/disadvantages of Python for data science

        Python is one of the most popular languages for data science due to the language's high-level nature, portability, and broad community support. The readability of the language, and the portability of running a Python script easily on different computers, enables collaboration that outweighs performance concerns. Additionally, industry professionals frequently contribute free and high-quality packages for data science that are widely used.

        Table 30.3.1: Advantages and disadvantages of Python for data science.
        Advantages Disadvantages
        Readability: Python reads like English, and functions from the same library use consistent syntax. Consistency: Different libraries may have different syntax conventions.
        Popularity: Python is popular in data science and elsewhere in industry, which means resources for learning Python are widely available. Memory: Python uses more computer memory than other programming languages.
        Innovation: New data science models and technologies are constantly added to Python. Speed: Other programming languages such as Julia perform computations on datasets more quickly than Python.
        Feedback?

        Feedback?

        Common data science packages

        Many Python packages exist for data manipulation, visualization, and modeling. Different packages provide different functionality, so a data science project will use multiple packages. Ex: Imagine a scientist wants to classify hawk populations in Iowa from a large dataset. First the data is loaded into special data structures using pandas, then classification algorithms are run from scikit-learn, and then the results are visualized using seaborn. The unique capabilities of each package provide a data scientist with a comprehensive set of tools for almost any task.

        Table 30.3.2: Common data science packages in Python.

        pandas pd pandas provides methods and classes for tabular and time-series data.
        sklearn sk scikit-learn provides implementations of many machine learning algorithms with a uniform syntax for preprocessing data, specifying models, fitting models with cross-validation, and assessing models.
        matplotlib.pyplot plt Matplotlib allows the creation of data visualizations in Python. The functions mostly expect NumPy arrays.
        seaborn sns seaborn also allows the creation of data visualizations but works better with pandas DataFrame objects.
        scipy.stats sp.stats SciPy provides algorithms and functions for computing problems that arise in science, engineering and statistics. scipy.stats provides the functions for statistics.
        statsmodels sm statsmodels adds functionality to Python to estimate many different kinds of statistical models, make inferences from those models, and explore data.

          30.4 Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks

          Jupyter

          Jupyter is an interactive development environment (IDE) for writing and testing code in data science and scientific computing. In Jupyter, code is written in an interactive document called a Jupyter notebook. A notebook contains cells, which organize code, text, and output all in one place for testing, presenting, and sharing. The three types of cells are code cells, markdown (text) cells, and raw (output) cells. Each cell can be run independently.

Exercise: Collaborative Document Editing

  1. Create a Repository

    • Student A creates a new repository on GitHub and initializes it with a README file.

  2. Invite Collaborator

    • Student A invites Student B to the repository as a collaborator.

  3. Create a New Branch

    • Both students create their own branches from the main branch. Let’s say Student A creates a branch named student-a-edits and Student B creates student-b-edits.

  4. Make Changes

    • Each student makes some changes to the README file in their respective branches. They can add some text or modify the existing content.

  5. Commit and Push Changes

    • After making the changes, each student commits the changes with a suitable commit message and pushes the changes to their respective branches on GitHub.

  6. Create Pull Requests

    • Both students create a pull request to merge their branches into the main branch. In the pull request description, they can describe the changes they made.

  7. Review Pull Requests

    • Each student reviews the other’s pull request, adds comments if necessary, and if everything looks good, they approve the pull request.

  8. Merge Pull Requests

    • After approval, each student merges the other’s pull request. If there are any merge conflicts, they will need to resolve them before the merge can be completed.

  9. Pull Changes

    • Finally, both students pull the changes from the main branch to their local repositories to get the latest version of the README file.

 

 

And here is a more fun version:

Exercise: The Great Cookie Caper

  1. Create a Repository

    • Student A creates a new repository on GitHub named “CookieCaper” and initializes it with a README file.

  2. Invite Collaborator

    • Student A invites Student B to the repository as a collaborator.

  3. Create a New Branch

    • Both students create their own branches from the main branch. Let’s say Student A creates a branch named cookie-design and Student B creates bank-plan.

  4. Make Changes

    • Student A adds a recipe for the special cookie in the cookie-design branch.
    • Student B outlines a silly plan for the bank heist in the bank-plan branch.

  5. Commit and Push Changes

    • After making the changes, each student commits the changes with a suitable commit message and pushes the changes to their respective branches on GitHub.

  6. Create Pull Requests

    • Both students create a pull request to merge their branches into the main branch. They review each other’s work and suggest changes.

  7. Merge Pull Requests

    • After reviewing and approving the changes, they merge the pull requests. Now, the main branch has both the cookie recipe and the bank heist plan.

And here’s a cheat sheet for Git:

Git Cheat Sheet

  • git init: Initialize a new Git repository.
  • git clone [url]: Clone a repository that exists on GitHub.
  • git branch [branch-name]: Create a new branch.
  • git checkout [branch-name]: Switch to a specific branch.
  • git add [file-name]: Add a file to the staging area.
  • git commit -m “[commit message]”: Commit changes with a message.
  • git push origin [branch-name]: Push changes to a remote repository.
  • git pull origin [branch-name]: Update local repository to the newest commit.
  • git merge [branch-name]: Merge a branch into the active branch.

Remember, Git is a powerful tool for team collaboration. It allows multiple people to work on a project without overwriting each other’s changes. Happy coding!

Instructions: Set Up and Clone the Repository for Collaboration Using Visual Studio Code

Follow these steps to create the repository on GitHub, set up collaborators and branches, and clone it into Visual Studio Code.

1. Set Up the Repository Online

  1. Create the Repository:

    • Go to GitHub and log in.
    • Click the + icon (top-right) and select New repository.
    • Fill in the details:
      • Repository name: funny-story-git-collaboration
      • Description: "A collaborative project to write a humorous story using Markdown and Git workflows."
      • Choose Public or Private as needed.
      • Check:
        • Add a README file
        • Add .gitignore: Select the Python template.
        • Add a license: Choose MIT License.
    • Click Create repository.

  2. Add Collaborators:

    • Open the repository, go to Settings > Collaborators and Teams > Manage Access.
    • Click Invite Collaborator and search for team members by their GitHub username or email. Assign appropriate permissions.

  3. Create Branches Online:

    • Go to the Code tab of your repository.
    • Click the main branch dropdown, type dev, and press Enter to create the branch.
    • Repeat this process to create any additional branches like feature/story-outline or feature/story-draft.

2. Clone the Repository Using Visual Studio Code

  1. Open Visual Studio Code:

    • Launch Visual Studio Code on your computer.

  2. Install Git (if not already installed):

    • Download and install Git from git-scm.com if needed.

  3. Clone the Repository:

    • In VS Code, open the Command Palette by pressing:
      • Ctrl + Shift + P (Windows/Linux) or Cmd + Shift + P (Mac).
    • Search for Git: Clone and select it.
    • Paste the repository URL (e.g., https://github.com/yourusername/funny-story-git-collaboration) and press Enter.
    • Choose a folder on your computer to save the repository.

  4. Open the Repository:

    • When cloning is complete, click Open in the prompt to open the repository in VS Code.
    • If no prompt appears, use File > Open Folder to navigate to the repository folder.
  5. Configure your user name and email
    1. Set your username: git config --global user.name "FIRST_NAME LAST_NAME" 
    2. Set your email address: git config --global user.email "MY_NAME@example.com"

3. Set Up the Environment in VS Code

  1. Switch to the dev Branch:

    • Open the integrated terminal in VS Code by pressing:
      • Ctrl + `` (backtick) (Windows/Linux) or `Cmd + `` (Mac).
    • Run: 
      git checkout dev

  2. Verify the Setup:

    • Open the Source Control View (shortcut: Ctrl + Shift + G or Cmd + Shift + G).
    • Ensure the repository files are visible, and the dev branch is active.

4. Start Contributing

  • Create or edit files (e.g., story.md, CONTRIBUTORS.md).
  • Stage and commit your changes using the built-in Git tools in VS Code or the terminal: 
    git add .
git commit -m "Your commit message"
git push origin dev

Tips for Smooth Collaboration

  • Review Branches: Use the GitHub website or git branch -a in the terminal to see all branches.
  • Collaborate Online: Open pull requests (PRs) on GitHub to merge changes into the dev or main branches.
  • Extensions: Install:
    • GitHub Pull Requests and Issues for GitHub integration.
    • Markdown Preview Enhanced to preview story.md.

This streamlined process sets up your repository for efficient collaboration and development!

 

This adjusted assignment introduces humor while ensuring students engage deeply with Git concepts and Markdown syntax!

CS2 Final Project – Data Explorer (Sorting & Searching Capstone)

1. Project Overview

For the last part of the semester, you’ll build a small “Data Explorer” program in Python.

Your program will:

  • Load a dataset from a file (CSV or text)

  • Store it using lists, dictionaries, and classes

  • Let a user search, sort, and filter the data through a simple menu

  • Create at least one plot to visualize something interesting

  • Handle bad input and file errors gracefully

This is not meant to be a huge stressful project. It’s a chance to use the tools you already know (loops, functions, classes, files, exceptions, searching, sorting, plotting) in one coherent program.

You will work individually but we’ll spend several class days doing pair programming and show-and-tell so you can get help and share ideas.

2. Learning Goals

By the end of this project, you should be able to:

  1. Design a small Python program using functions, modules, and classes.

  2. Use lists and dictionaries to store structured data.

  3. Read from and write to files in a safe way.

  4. Implement and use simple searching and sorting algorithms.

  5. Add basic exception handling to make your program robust.

  6. Create a simple plot from your data and interpret it.

  7. Talk about your design choices and reflect on what you learned.

3. What You Will Build

You will choose a dataset (or use one provided) such as:

  • Movies (title, year, rating, genre)

  • Songs (title, artist, length, rating)

  • Students (name, major, GPA, graduation year)

  • Books, video games, sports stats, etc.

Then you’ll build a terminal-based Data Explorer that supports at least:

  • Loading the data from a file into memory

  • Showing a list of records (possibly limited to top N)

  • Searching for records by some key (title, name, ID, etc.)

  • Sorting the data by at least one field

  • Saving some results (for example, a filtered or sorted subset) to a file

  • Generating one simple plot (e.g., a bar chart or histogram)

4. Project Requirements

4.1 Data & Model

  • Your program must read from at least one input file (CSV or reasonably structured text).

  • Create at least one class to represent a record, e.g.:

    class Movie:
    def __init__(self, title, year, rating, genre):
        ...

  • Store your data in a list of objects (or dictionaries).

4.2 Program Structure

  • Your code must be split into at least two modules:

    • models.py – classes and any data-related helper functions

    • app.py – user interface (menus, main loop)

  • Use functions to organize your code. Avoid writing all logic in one giant main().

4.3 Core Features

Your program must support:

  1. Menu-based interface

    • A loop that repeatedly shows options (list data, search, sort, plot, quit).

    • Clear prompts and labels.

  2. Searching

    • Implement at least one search algorithm yourself:

      • Linear search is fine.

      • If you want to use binary search, make sure the data is sorted first.

    • Use your search in at least one menu option (e.g., “Find movie by title”).

  3. Sorting

    • Implement at least one simple sort yourself (e.g. insertion sort or selection sort).

    • Also demonstrate Python’s built-in sorted() on the same data.

    • You should be able to tell the user which sort is being used in each option.

  4. Files

    • Use with open(...) to read your data file.

    • Provide at least one option that writes out data (e.g. saving a filtered or sorted list to a new file).

  5. Exceptions & Robustness

    • Use try/except to handle:

      • Invalid user input (e.g. non-integer menu choices)

      • Missing or unreadable file

    • Program should not crash on simple user mistakes.

  6. Plotting

    • Use a plotting library (such as matplotlib) to draw at least one plot related to your data:

      • Example: histogram of ratings, bar chart of counts per genre/major, etc.

    • The plot can appear in a separate window or be saved as an image file.

4.4 Reflection

Write a short reflection (roughly ½–1 page) that answers:

  • What data did you choose, and why?

  • Which searching and sorting strategies did you implement?

  • One thing that surprised you while building the project.

  • If you had one more week, what would you add or improve?

You may submit this as a text file, PDF, or Canvas text entry.

4.5 Optional Extensions (Bonus / Stretch)

These are not required, but can earn bonus credit and make your project more interesting:

  • Inheritance (e.g. MediaItem base class with Movie and Song subclasses).

  • Use binary search on a sorted list.

  • Add multiple plots or more advanced visualizations.

  • Add simple unit tests for your search/sort functions.

  • Use basic recursion somewhere reasonable (not forced).

5. Timeline & In-Class Plan

This is a Monday/Wednesday/Friday class.

Week 1 – Kickoff & Planning (This Week)

Day 1 (Today) – Project Overview & Kickoff

  • Project handout and explanation.

  • In-class:

    • Choose or explore possible datasets.

    • Sketch your data model (what fields each record has).

    • Start a basic project folder with app.py and models.py.

Day 2 (Wednesday) – Pair Programming #1

  • Focus: data loading + basic menu.

  • In-class goals:

    • Define your main data class in models.py.

    • Write code to load the file into a list of objects.

    • Add a simple main menu and an option to print the first few records.

Day 3 (Friday) – Project Plan Show & Tell

  • Each student (or small team if you’re sharing data) will very briefly:

    • Introduce their dataset.

    • Explain their planned features (search + sort + plot).

    • Show whatever they already have working (even if it’s just data loading).

Week 2 – Thanksgiving Week (Campus Partially Closed)

  • Monday: Optional office hours / help session.

  • Wednesday & Friday: No class (Thanksgiving break).

No new required work is assigned this week.
You may use this time to make progress if you want, but you are not required to.

Week 3 – Build, Polish, and Demo (Week After Thanksgiving / Dead Week)

Day 4 (Monday) – Pair Programming #2

  • Focus: searching and sorting.

  • In-class goals:

    • Implement your required search function.

    • Implement your required sort function.

    • Integrate both into your menu.

Day 5 (Wednesday) – Pair Programming #3

  • Focus: exceptions, plotting, and polish.

  • In-class goals:

    • Wrap user input and file operations with try/except.

    • Add at least one plot.

    • Clean up your menu and output formatting.

    • Work on your short reflection.

Day 6 (Friday) – Final Show & Tell

  • Each student gives a 3–5 minute demo:

    • Run your program and show:

      • Data loading

      • One search

      • One sort

      • Your plot

    • Share one thing you’re proud of and one challenge you hit.

  • Final project files and reflection are due Friday night (or whatever deadline your instructor sets).

6. Deliverables

By the final deadline, you will submit:

  1. Code

    • All .py files needed to run your project.

    • Your data file(s) (unless they are huge; in that case, include a small sample).

  2. Reflection

    • ½–1 page answering the questions in Section 4.4.

  3. Demo

    • In-class show-and-tell on the two Fridays:

      • Week 1 Friday – project plan.

      • Week 3 Friday – final project demo.

7. Grading Rubric (100 points + optional bonus)

1. Core Functionality (50 points)

  • Loads data from file into appropriate structures (10)

  • Menu-driven interface with at least three meaningful options (10)

  • Working search feature using your own implementation (10)

  • Working sort feature using your own implementation + use of sorted() somewhere (10)

  • Ability to save some results to a file (10)

2. Use of CS2 Concepts (25 points)

  • Proper use of at least one class to model records (10)

  • Use of modules and functions to organize code (5)

  • Basic exception handling for input and files (5)

  • At least one plot generated from your data (5)

3. Code Quality & Style (15 points)

  • Reasonable variable and function names (5)

  • Code is broken into functions instead of one giant block (5)

  • Comments/docstrings where needed; code is readable (5)

4. Communication & Reflection (10 points)

  • Participation in the two show-and-tell days (5)

  • Clear, honest written reflection turned in on time (5)

Bonus / Stretch Features (up to +10 points)

  • Any combination of optional extensions (inheritance, binary search, extra plots, tests, recursion, etc.) that are well-implemented and documented.

assignments.description:
Objective: The goal of this assignment is to enhance your programming skills through collaboration with peers or with AI assistance. You will learn to tackle coding challenges effectively, whether by working with a classmate or by utilizing ChatGPT as a learning partner. This assignment emphasizes not just solving the problem but also understanding the process and best practices for learning how to program.

Assignment Overview:

  1. In-Class Pair Programming (Double Points):
    • Work with a classmate to complete the programming assignment.
    • One person will be the “driver” (the person typing the code), and the other will be the “navigator” (the person reviewing and suggesting improvements).
    • You should switch roles regularly to ensure both partners contribute equally to the task.
    • At the end of the session, submit your solution with:
      • The name of your partner.
      • A brief statement of who had fingers on the keyboard and how the roles were divided.
  2. ChatGPT as a Programming Partner (Full Points):
    • If you choose to work independently, you may use ChatGPT as your programming partner.
    • Engage in a meaningful dialogue with ChatGPT to solve the assignment, asking questions, exploring different approaches, and learning new concepts.
    • Submit the full transcript of your ChatGPT interaction along with your solution.

Best Practices:

For Pair Programming:

  • Communication: Regularly discuss your thought process with your partner. Clear communication will help you both understand the problem better and develop a shared solution.
  • Weekly Role Assignment: Each week, one partner will take on the role of the “driver” (the person typing the code), while the other will be the “navigator” (the person reviewing and suggesting improvements). Only the driver should be actively working on the code during that week’s assignment.
  • Partners should alternate roles each week so that both of you gain experience in both driving and mentoring.
  • Respect and Patience: Listen to your partner’s ideas, and be open to different approaches. Be patient, especially if your partner is struggling with a concept.
  • Reflection: After completing the assignment, take a few minutes to discuss what you learned, what challenges you faced, and how you overcame them.

For Using ChatGPT:

  • Ask Detailed Questions: Don’t just ask for the solution. Instead, ask ChatGPT to explain concepts, provide examples, or suggest alternative approaches.
  • Understand the Code: Before moving forward, make sure you understand every line of code provided by ChatGPT. Ask follow-up questions if something is unclear.
  • Experiment: Use ChatGPT to explore different ways of solving the problem. Try out variations of the code and ask about the pros and cons of each approach.
  • Learn by Teaching: Explain your understanding to ChatGPT. Teaching back to the AI can reinforce your learning and highlight any gaps in your knowledge.

Submission Requirements:

  • In-Class Pair Programming: Submit the names of both partners, the division of roles, and a brief reflection on the experience.
    • Optional: Instead of a brief text entry, you can upload a video summarizing your collaboration and discussing your roles.
  • ChatGPT Transcript: Submit your code along with the full transcript of your interaction with ChatGPT and a brief reflection on what you learned.

Grading: This assignment is graded on a pass-fail basis. However, those who submit a complete in-class pair programming assignment will receive double points as a bonus. Your submission should demonstrate a clear understanding of the problem and a thoughtful approach to learning.

# Coding Odyssey 1

**Instructor: Jeremy Evert**  
**Contact: Email - jeremy.evert@swosu.edu | Text - 785-443-0967**  

## Objective:
This assignment aims to encourage you to apply the programming concepts and tools you have learned in class to build a project of your choice. The goal is to foster creativity, problem-solving, and practical application of theoretical knowledge.

## Assignment Guidelines:

1. **Project Selection**:
   - Choose a project idea that interests you. It can be a game, a utility, a simulation, or any other application.
   - Ensure that your project incorporates most of the concepts we have covered in class, including but not limited to:
     - Variables and Data Types
     - Control Structures (loops, conditionals)
     - Functions and Modular Programming
     - Basic Data Structures (lists, dictionaries)
     - File I/O
     - Error Handling
     - (Optional) Basic GUI elements (if you wish to explore)

2. **Design Phase**:
   - **Design Document**: Create a design document outlining the following:
     - **Project Title**: Name of your project.
     - **Description**: A brief overview of what your project does.
     - **Features**: List the main features of your project.
     - **Tools/Technologies**: Identify the tools, libraries, and languages you will use.
     - **Flowchart/Diagram**: Provide a flowchart or diagram of your program’s architecture.
     - **Milestones**: Break down your project into smaller tasks or milestones.

3. **Implementation Phase**:
   - Start coding your project based on your design document.
   - Ensure that you write clean, readable, and well-documented code.
   - Use version control (e.g., Git) to track your progress and changes.

4. **Testing and Debugging**:
   - Test your code regularly to catch and fix bugs early.
   - Ensure that your code handles errors gracefully and includes appropriate error messages.

5. **Final Submission**:
   - Submit the following:
     - **Design Document**: Updated if there were any changes during implementation.
     - **Source Code**: All the code files of your project.
     - **Readme File**: Instructions on how to run your project, any dependencies, and a brief user guide.
     - **Demonstration**: (Optional) A short video or presentation demonstrating your project.

## Grading Structure:

- **Base Points (Not Stacking)**:
  - **25 Points**: You have a design for your idea.
  - **50 Points**: You have a design and some code.
  - **75 Points**: You have a design and some of your code runs.
  - **100 Points**: You have a design and a working code.

- **Bonus Points**:
  - **Creativity**: Innovative and original ideas.
  - **Efficiency**: Optimal use of resources and efficient algorithms.
  - **Enjoyment**: Fun and engaging user experience.
  - **Clean Code**: Well-structured, commented, and readable code.

## Submission:
- Submit your project through the course’s submission portal or email it directly to jeremy.evert@swosu.edu by the due date.

## Tips for Success:
- **Plan Ahead**: Start with a clear plan and follow it.
- **Stay Organized**: Keep your code and resources well-organized.
- **Seek Help**: If you encounter any issues, feel free to reach out for help.
- **Experiment and Learn**: Don’t be afraid to try new things and learn from them.

Good luck, and happy coding!

---

# Coding Odyssey 3

**Instructor: Jeremy Evert**  
**Contact: Email - jeremy.evert@swosu.edu | Text - 785-443-0967**  

## Objective:
This assignment aims to encourage you to apply the programming concepts and tools you have learned in class to build a project of your choice. The goal is to foster creativity, problem-solving, and practical application of theoretical knowledge.

## Assignment Guidelines:

1. **Project Selection**:
   - Choose a project idea that interests you. It can be a game, a utility, a simulation, or any other application.
   - Ensure that your project incorporates most of the concepts we have covered in class, including but not limited to:
     - Variables and Data Types
     - Control Structures (loops, conditionals)
     - Functions and Modular Programming
     - Basic Data Structures (lists, dictionaries)
     - File I/O
     - Error Handling
     - (Optional) Basic GUI elements (if you wish to explore)

2. **Design Phase**:
   - **Design Document**: Create a design document outlining the following:
     - **Project Title**: Name of your project.
     - **Description**: A brief overview of what your project does.
     - **Features**: List the main features of your project.
     - **Tools/Technologies**: Identify the tools, libraries, and languages you will use.
     - **Flowchart/Diagram**: Provide a flowchart or diagram of your program’s architecture.
     - **Milestones**: Break down your project into smaller tasks or milestones.

3. **Implementation Phase**:
   - Start coding your project based on your design document.
   - Ensure that you write clean, readable, and well-documented code.
   - Use version control (e.g., Git) to track your progress and changes.

4. **Testing and Debugging**:
   - Test your code regularly to catch and fix bugs early.
   - Ensure that your code handles errors gracefully and includes appropriate error messages.

5. **Final Submission**:
   - Submit the following:
     - **Design Document**: Updated if there were any changes during implementation.
     - **Source Code**: All the code files of your project.
     - **Readme File**: Instructions on how to run your project, any dependencies, and a brief user guide.
     - **Demonstration**: (Optional) A short video or presentation demonstrating your project.

## Grading Structure:

- **Base Points (Not Stacking)**:
  - **25 Points**: You have a design for your idea.
  - **50 Points**: You have a design and some code.
  - **75 Points**: You have a design and some of your code runs.
  - **100 Points**: You have a design and a working code.

- **Bonus Points**:
  - **Creativity**: Innovative and original ideas.
  - **Efficiency**: Optimal use of resources and efficient algorithms.
  - **Enjoyment**: Fun and engaging user experience.
  - **Clean Code**: Well-structured, commented, and readable code.

## Submission:
- Submit your project through the course’s submission portal or email it directly to jeremy.evert@swosu.edu by the due date.

## Tips for Success:
- **Plan Ahead**: Start with a clear plan and follow it.
- **Stay Organized**: Keep your code and resources well-organized.
- **Seek Help**: If you encounter any issues, feel free to reach out for help.
- **Experiment and Learn**: Don’t be afraid to try new things and learn from them.

Good luck, and happy coding!

Unofficial Transcript Assignment: Unofficial Transcript.docx

 

Hey everyone! Welcome to the start of the semester. I'm thrilled to embark on this academic adventure with you. Remember, you have the power to take charge of your own success. Don't hesitate to reach out to me if you need any help along the way. By taking ownership of your studies, you'll gain confidence, perform better academically, and set yourself up for success after graduation. Let's make this semester great together!

 

As we start this journey, it's important to review your academic progress towards graduation. Your official university academic record is called your transcript. For this exercise, we'll begin with your unofficial transcript. Remember, this assignment is not just about earning points. It's a chance to take a close look at your academic progress, think about the classes you want to take, and set goals for your GPA. By examining your unofficial transcript, you'll get a clearer picture of where you stand and what you can do to achieve your academic goals. Here's a step-by-step guide to help you through the process:

Step-by-Step Guide to Reviewing Your Unofficial Transcript

  1. Obtain Your Unofficial Transcript:
    • Log in to your student portal.
    • Navigate to the section where you can view or download your unofficial transcript.
    • Download a digital copy of your transcript. This is what is graded for your assignment.
  1. Check Course Enrollment:
    • Compare the courses you are currently enrolled in with your transcript.
    • Ensure you are not enrolled in any courses for which you have already received credit.
    • Note any discrepancies, such as being enrolled in a course you have previously completed successfully.
  1. Verify Grades:
    • Review the grades listed for each course.
    • Confirm that the grades match your expectations based on your performance.
    • Highlight any grades that are not what you expected or are missing.
    • Reach out to the instructor for any class with a problem. Ask them what their grade change policy is.

 


  • Review Tuition and Credits:
  • Check that all courses you have paid tuition for are listed on the transcript.
  • Ensure that all credits you have earned are accurately reflected.
  • Verify that there are no missing courses or discrepancies in credit hours.
  • Identify Unexpected Items:
  • Look for any courses, grades, or credits that are unexpected.
  • Make a note of any anomalies or surprises that need further investigation.
  • Reach out to your advisor or academic records in the Registrar’s office and find out what you can about anything that does not make sense to you.
  • Document Your Findings:
  • Create a list of any issues or unexpected findings from your review.
  • Include details such as the course name, expected vs. actual grade, and any discrepancies in enrollment or credits.
  • Contact Your Instructor:
  • Prepare an email or text message to your instructor with your findings.
  • Be clear and concise, providing specific details about the discrepancies.

Email Template

Here’s a sample email template you can use to report any discrepancies to your instructor:

 


Subject: Discrepancies Found in Unofficial Transcript

Dear Professor Evert,

I have reviewed my unofficial transcript closely and have identified a few discrepancies that I need your assistance with:

  1. Duplicate Course Enrollment:
    • Course: [Course Name]
    • Issue: I am currently enrolled in this course but have already received credit for it previously.
  1. Unexpected Grades:
    • Course: [Course Name]
    • Expected Grade: [Expected Grade]
    • Actual Grade: [Actual Grade]
  1. Missing Course/Credit:
    • Course: [Course Name]
    • Issue: This course, for which I have paid tuition, is missing from my transcript.

I have attached a copy of my unofficial transcript for your reference. Please let me know how we can resolve these issues.

Thank you for your assistance.

Best regards, [Your Name] [Your Student ID]

 

 

Text Message Template

 

If you prefer to send a text message, here’s a shorter version:

 


Hi Prof. Evert, this is [Your Name, Student ID]. I've found a few discrepancies in my unofficial transcript:

  1. Duplicate course enrollment in [Course Name].
  2. Unexpected grade in [Course Name] (Expected: [Grade], Actual: [Grade]).
  3. Missing course/credit for [Course Name]. Please advise on how to resolve these. Thanks!


Final Steps

  • Send Your Communication: Your teacher for this class cannot change your grade for a previous class. Email or text your previous instructor with the documented discrepancies.
  • Follow Up: If you do not receive a response within a few days, follow up with another email or text to ensure your concerns are addressed.

By carefully reviewing your unofficial transcript and promptly addressing any issues with your instructor, you can ensure that your academic record is accurate and complete.

Resume assignment link: Resume.docx

 

### Resume Assignment

For this assignment, you will create or update your resume to reflect your current work experience, education, and accomplishments. Your resume will be a living document that you will continue to build on throughout the semester. Follow the instructions below to complete the assignment and make your resume stand out.

### Assignment Instructions

1. **Create or Update Your Resume:**
   - Include sections for contact information, work experience, education, skills, and accomplishments.
   - If you are a recent high school graduate, include relevant high school achievements. If you have been out of school for a while, focus on more recent accomplishments.

2. **Save and Maintain Your Resume:**
   - Save your resume as a digital document. You will be adding to it and refining it throughout the semester.

3. **Seek Feedback:**
   - Visit Career Services or the Writing Center for assistance with your resume.
   - Ask your advisor, teachers, and mentors from your community to review your resume and provide feedback.
   - Consider watching LinkedIn Learning videos on resume writing for additional tips.

4. **Use the 3-2-1 Plan for Continuous Improvement:**
   - **Daily:** Set an alarm to spend five minutes writing down three things you accomplished that day.
   - **Weekly:** Set a calendar reminder to spend 30 minutes adding two things you achieved that week to your Curriculum Vitae (CV).
   - **Monthly:** Set a monthly calendar reminder to dedicate an hour to updating your resume, adding at least one new bullet point each month.

### Tips and Tricks for a Great Resume

- **Tailor Your Resume:** Customize your resume for each job application by highlighting the most relevant experience and skills.
- **Use Action Verbs:** Start each bullet point with a strong action verb (e.g., "developed," "managed," "led") to convey your achievements effectively.
- **Quantify Achievements:** Whenever possible, use numbers to quantify your accomplishments (e.g., "Increased sales by 20%" or "Managed a team of 10").
- **Keep It Concise:** Aim for a one-page resume if you have less than 10 years of experience. Ensure it is easy to read with clear headings and bullet points.
- **Professional Appearance:** Use a clean, professional format with consistent fonts and spacing. Avoid using overly decorative elements that may distract from the content.

### Submission

- Save your resume as a PDF.
- Upload the PDF to the assignment submission section.

### Points: 10

### Due Date

- **Available:** January 16 at 12am
- **Due:** January 22 at 5pm
- **Until:** May 9 at 11:59pm

If you have any questions or encounter any issues, please email me at jeremy.evert@swosu.edu or text me at 785-443-0967. 

### Resume Feedback

Consider taking your resume to the Writing Center in the Library and Career Services for additional support. Engage with mentors, advisors, and instructors for constructive feedback. Regularly update and refine your resume using the 3-2-1 plan to ensure it accurately reflects your progress and achievements.

### Dream Job Paper Assignment

For this assignment, I want you to think seriously about your dream job. This isn't just a hypothetical exercise—I want you to identify a real job that you could apply for and discuss why it is your dream job and why it is important to you.

### Assignment Instructions

1. **Choose a Specific Dream Job:**
   - Identify a real job that you aspire to have. Make sure it is a position you could realistically apply for, whether now or in the future.

2. **Research the Job:**
   - Investigate the job's requirements, including education, skills, experience, and other qualifications.
   - Look into the responsibilities, typical work environment, and career advancement opportunities associated with the job.

3. **Write an Essay Discussing the Following:**

   b. **How it Aligns with Your Skills and Interests:**

      - Reflect on how achieving this dream job would influence your professional and personal life.
      - Consider the benefits such as career satisfaction, financial stability, personal growth, and work-life balance.

- **Length:** 2-3 pages, double-spaced
